title: Exploitation of CVE-2024-35250 via MSKSSRV Kernel Driver
id: 5a8b7c9d-1e2f-4a5b-8c9d-1e2f4a5b8c9d
status: experimental
description: Detects exploitation attempts of CVE-2024-35250 by monitoring for crafted IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY requests with KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET flag sent to MSKSSRV driver.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2024/12/cisa-and-fbi-raise-alerts-on-exploited.html
    - https://devco.re/blog/2024/08/23/streaming-vulnerabilities-from-windows-kernel-proxying-to-kernel-part1-en/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-25
tags:
    - attack.privilege_escalation
    - attack.t1068
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith: '\mskssrv.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY'
            - 'KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET'
            - 'KSPROPSETID_DrmAudioStream'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative tools using kernel streaming APIs
level: high

pipeline.attack_summary: An attacker exploits a local untrusted pointer dereference vulnerability (CVE-2024-35250) in the Microsoft Kernel Streaming Service (MSKSSRV) driver to escalate privileges. The attack leverages IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY with KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET flag, triggering a double-fetch issue that allows arbitrary kernel code execution via crafted input buffers. This enables privilege escalation from user to system level.

indicators.context: Microsoft Windows Kernel-Mode Driver contains an untrusted pointer dereference vulnerability that allows a local attacker to escalate privileges (Patched by Microsoft in June 2024)

Taiwanese cybersecurity company DEVCORE, which discovered and reported CVE-2024-35250, shared additional technical details in August 2024, stating it's rooted in the Microsoft Kernel Streaming Service (MSKSSRV)
ksthunk.sys is the entry point in Kernel Streaming. Its function is quite simple: it converts 32-bit requests from the WoW64 process into 64-bit requests
ks.sys is one of the core components of Kernel Streaming. It is the library of Kernel Streaming responsible for forwarding requests such as IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY to the corresponding device driver

Port class driver mostly used for PCI and DMA-based audio device hardware drivers. Currently, most audio-related processing, such as volume control or microphone-related processing, falls into this category. The main component library used would be portcls.sys

Each of these KS objects will have its own property, and each property corresponds to a specific feature. These properties typically correspond to a set of GUIDs. We can set these properties through IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY

If we give the property set as KSPROPSETID_DrmAudioStream, there is additional processing at [5]. At [6], we can see that it first checks whether Irp->RequestorMode is KernelMode(0). If it is called from user, it will directly return an error

In the IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY of Kernel Streaming, to increase efficiency, KSPROPERTY_TYPE_SERIALIZESET and KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET requests are provided to allow users to operate on multiple properties through a single call
hr = KsOpenDefaultDevice(KSCATEGORY_VIDEO_CAMERA,GENERIC_READ|GENERIC_WRITE, &g_hDevice)

status = KsSynchronousIoControlDevice(CurrentStackLocation->FileObject, 0, CurrentStackLocation->Parameters.DeviceIoControl.IoControlCode, New_KsProperty_req, InSize, OutBuffer, OutSize, &BytesReturned)
When we initially send IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY, we use the existing property KSPROPSETID_Service of MSKSSRV for subsequent operations

However, we will not be explaining these vulnerabilities one by one. Most of these are obvious issues such as unchecked length or index leading to out-of-bounds access. @Fr0st1706 also wrote an exploit for CVE-2024-38054 recently
portcls.sys CVE-2024-38055 (out-of-bounds read when set dataformat for Pin) CVE-2024-38056
portcls.sys CVE-2024-38055 (out-of-bounds read when set dataformat for Pin) CVE-2024-38056

After re-examining, it was found that IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY uses Neither I/O to transmit data, which means it uses the input buffer for data processing directly. Generally speaking, this method is not recommended as it often leads to double fetch issues. ... From the above figure of KspPropertyHandler, we can see that after the user calls IOCTL, the Type3InputBuffer is directly copied into a newly allocated buffer, containing the KSPROPERTY structure

When the target user runs Winbox Loader software (a utility used for Mikrotik router configuration), this connects to the router and downloads some DLLs (dynamic link libraries) from the router’s file system.

pipeline.attack_summary: An attacker uses phishing emails containing hyperlinks to deliver a NetWire RAT variant via MediaFire. The malware is delivered as a 7z archive that decompresses into an EXE file named 'PROFORMA-INVOICE 0990.exe'. The malware employs anti-analysis techniques including dynamic code extraction, mouse movement detection for sandbox evasion, and anti-debugging measures. It relocates itself to %AppData%\Install\Host.exe, creates registry persistence under HKCU\SOFTWARE\NetWire, collects system information, logs keystrokes, and communicates with a C2 server at gbam0001.duckdns.org:3366 using a custom protocol.

indicators.context: The downloaded file is a 7z file, which contains the new variant of NetWire RAT. After decompressing it, we are able to get an EXE file with the name of "PROFORMA-INVOICE 0990.exe".
The downloaded file is a 7z file, which contains the new variant of NetWire RAT.
As you can see, the malware file download link is: "hxxps[:]//www[.]mediafire[.]com/file/d86hz5qj21lmhrb/PROFORMA-INVOICE_0990.7z/file".

The new process then performs all of the above procedures again. Figure 5 is the screenshot of the process tree. You can see the process where NetWire was relocated to "C:\Users\user_name\AppData\Roaming\Install\Host.exe".
NetWire continues to create its home key (HKCU\SOFTWARE\NetWire) as well as adding it into the auto-run group in the victim's registry.
NetWire creates a log folder to store the log files of information that it collects from the victim's system. The log folder is located at "%AppData%\Logs".
It checks to see if the current executable file is located in the correct folder (%AppData%\Install) and has the right file name (Host.exe).
Its domain is found in the decrypted string, which for this variant is "gbam0001.duckdns[.]org:3366".

It also calls the API ntdll.ZwGetContextThread to obtain the current thread context structure, which contains the CPU debug register status.

rules_yaml:
title: Initial Access - Commvault Command Injection via Unauthenticated Login
id: 5a8c2d4e-3b6f-4a9c-8d1e-2f4a7b9c1d3e
status: experimental
description: Detects initial access through unauthenticated HTTP POST to /commandcenter/api/Login with crafted commserver parameter enabling command injection in qlogin command.
references:
    - https://labs.watchtowr.com/guess-who-would-be-stupid-enough-to-rob-the-same-vault-twice-pre-auth-rce-chains-in-commvault/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-25
tags:
    - attack.initial_access
    - attack.t1078.004
    - attack.t1566.001
logsource:
    category: webserver
    product: apache
    service: httpd
detection:
    selection_method:
        cs-method: POST
    selection_path:
        cs-uri-query: /commandcenter/api/Login
    selection_body:
        request_body|contains:
            - '"commserver":".*-cs .*"'
    condition: all of selection_ *
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using commserver parameter with -cs argument
level: high

title: Privilege Escalation - Qlogin Command Execution with Localadmin Argument
id: 9f2d8e4a-1c3b-4d5e-6f7a-8b9c0d1e2f3a
status: experimental
description: Detects privilege escalation through execution of qlogin command with -localadmin argument, bypassing authentication to gain access to localadmin account.
references:
    - https://labs.watchtowr.com/guess-who-would-be-stupid-enough-to-rob-the-same-vault-twice-pre-auth-rce-chains-in-commvault/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-25
tags:
    - attack.privilege_escalation
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1078.004
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_cmdline:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'qlogin -cs '
            - ' -gt -u '
            - ' -clp '
    selection_process:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\qlogin.exe'
            - '\qlogin'
    condition: all of selection_ *
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using qlogin with valid parameters
level: high

title: Execution - JSP Webshell Dropping via QCommand
id: 7b3c4d5e-6f1a-7b8c-9d0e-1f2a3b4c5d6e
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of commands that drop JSP webshells in the Commvault webroot, indicating remote code execution through command injection.
references:
    - https://labs.watchtowr.com/guess-who-would-be-stupid-enough-to-rob-the-same-vault-twice-pre-auth-rce-chains-in-commvault/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-25
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.t1059.007
    - attack.t1505.003
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_cmdline:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'qoperation execute -af '
            - '.jsp'
    selection_process:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\qoperation.exe'
            - '\qoperation'
    condition: all of selection_ *
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using qoperation with XML files
level: high

pipeline.attack_summary: Raspberry Robin is a worm that initially spread via infected USB drives containing LNK files disguised as folders. It leverages autorun.inf configurations and user interaction to execute malicious code, using living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) like cmd.exe, msiexec.exe, rundll32.exe, and regsvr32.exe for execution and persistence. The malware injects into system processes, connects to C2 servers hosted on Tor nodes, and persists via the RunOnce registry key. It has evolved to deploy other malware families such as FakeUpdates, IcedID, Bumblebee, and TrueBot, often leading to ransomware activity through follow-on hands-on-keyboard attacks.

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack began with exploitation of CVE-2023-27532 to gain unauthenticated access to Veeam Backup & Replication servers via TCP port 9401, leading to SQL shell command execution and PowerShell script download/execution using POWERTRASH loader. The threat actor then conducted reconnaissance, credential theft, and lateral movement before establishing persistence through a custom DUBLOADER mechanism involving side-loading of malicious libcurl.dll with embedded DICELOADER payload.

indicators.context: An SQL server process related to the Veeam Backup instance executed a shell command
The script contains an embedded payload that is executed through reflective PE injection. POWERTRASH is an obfuscated loader written in PowerShell that has been attributed to FIN7
The filenames (e.g. icsnd16_64refl.ps1, icbt11801_64refl.ps1) used for these PowerShell scripts were also (notably) identical to the naming convention reportedly used by FIN7
The filenames (e.g. icsnd16_64refl.ps1, icbt11801_64refl.ps1) used for these PowerShell scripts were also (notably) identical to the naming convention reportedly used by FIN7

The threat actor used a series of commands as well as custom scripts to gather host and network information from the compromised machines. Some of these commands included: tasklist
The threat actor used a series of commands as well as custom scripts to gather host and network information from the compromised machines. Some of these commands included: ipconfig

To resolve the list of collected IP addresses to their respective host names, a custom PowerShell script, "host_ip.ps1", was executed. The PowerShell script content is nearly identical to a code snippet shared online for resolving IP to Hostname with PowerShell

An additional file called "445.ps1" was dropped and executed on the compromised Veeam backup servers. The retrieved script content functions as a port checker, which tests whether a port is open for a given address by attempting to establish a socket connection
A custom PowerShell script, "gup18.ps1", was executed to set up an active foothold in the compromised machine by creating a persistence mechanism to execute DICELOADER on device startup

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files are: gup.exe – Legitimate GUP.exe binary (part of the Notepad++ application)
The dropped files are: gup.xml – Configuration file that’s part of the GUP application
libcurl.dll – .NET DLL file side-loaded by gup.exe
JZ4qWKZW – Encoded DICELOADER payload that’s loaded and executed by libcurl.dll
jkBDfXaL.bat – Batch file that executes gup.exe
0JNvHvAz.vbs – VBScript file that executes the batch file

The PowerShell script drops 7 files, which are embedded in the script content, into a unique folder in %APPDATA%, and sets an autorun registry entry to establish persistence. The dropped files are: ... JZ4qWKZW – Encoded DICELOADER payload that’s loaded and executed by libcurl.dll

The crafted loader is designed to mimic the legitimate libcurl.dll file by including export function names found in the legitimate version and thus imported by the GUP executable. Only one of the export functions, namely "curl_easy_init" contains malicious code. All other export functions are trivially implemented with "retn 0" instructions. The "curl_easy_init" export function, which implements the malicious code, is the first function from the library that is called by the GUP executable. Therefore, the malicious code is executed immediately when GUP.exe is launched. This unique loader has not been previously seen in FIN7’s attack arsenal, and we are now tracking it as DUBLOADER
This script performed remote injection into the ‘PlugPlay’ service, which made a network connection to a remote host on port 443
The affected servers had TCP open port 9401 exposed to the internet. This port is used for communication with the Veeam Backup Service over SSL

rules_yaml:
title: Initial Access - Unauthenticated OGNL Injection in Confluence
id: 5f8c7b4a-2d9e-4a1f-9b3c-8e6d7f1a2b3c
status: stable
description: Detects unauthenticated HTTP GET or POST requests to Confluence Server/Data Center endpoints with crafted OGNL expressions that trigger remote code execution via CVE-2021-26084.
references:
    - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-26084
    - https://confluence.atlassian.com/doc/confluence-security-advisory-2021-08-25-1077906215.html
    - https://github.com/h3v0x/CVE-2021-26084_Confluence
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1213/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1588/006/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-09-25
tags:
    - attack.initial_access
    - attack.t1213.001
logsource:
    category: webserver
    product: confluence
    service: http
detection:
    selection:
        cs-uri-stem: '/pages/createpage-entervariables.action'
        cs-method:
            - 'GET'
            - 'POST'
    keywords:
        - '${'
        - 'class.module.classLoader'
        - 'exec('
    condition: selection and keywords
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative access to Confluence management endpoints
    - Automated monitoring or scanning tools accessing the endpoint
level: critical
